card.flavorText: In 1941, the Soviet Union rushed to raise new forces as German armies advanced toward Moscow and Leningrad. In Moscow, twelve people’s militia divisions were formed in only a few days in July. Recruits came from factories, offices, schools, and institutes. The campaign was presented as voluntary, but local party and military officials also used lists from workplaces to fill the ranks quickly. This gave units strong local ties, yet it also caused some problems. Skilled workers, older men, students, and people with little military experience often ended up in frontline formations before proper screening and training could be completed. Leningrad followed a similar path. Its People’s Militia Army began forming in late June 1941 from workers, students, reserve officers, retired officers, and destruction battalions first meant to fight saboteurs and parachutists. Some militia units were later absorbed into regular Red Army formations. Alongside them, behind German lines, Soviet partisan recruits included civilians and escaped soldiers.
